templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Concession: grant, then the main claim resumes (but / Still)
Concession: supported claim, then a fact that qualifies it
Purpose and aptness: goal then deliberate act, or a fitting echo
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.passage: Maltese, the national language of Malta, descends from the Arabic dialect once spoken in medieval Sicily, and linguists accordingly classify it as a Semitic language. ______ more than half of its lexicon comes from Italian, Sicilian, and English, but its grammatical structure and its most basic everyday vocabulary remain Semitic. Its terms for numbers and kinship, for example, derive from Arabic.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives the classification: Maltese is a Semitic language. The blank sentence first admits a fact that seems to cut against that label (most of its words come from European languages) and then, with “but,” returns to the point that its grammar and core words are Semitic. “Of course” introduces a point the writer grants before turning back to the main claim.

A.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not reword the classification of Maltese as Semitic; its first half names the European sources of most of its words, a point the sentence then has to answer with “but.”

C.why_wrong: Being classified as Semitic does not cause Maltese to take most of its vocabulary from Italian, Sicilian, and English; the classification is not the reason for the borrowing.

D.why_wrong: “In addition” would add a further point in support of the Semitic classification, but heavy borrowing from European languages is a reason to doubt the label, which is why the sentence needs its own “but.”

items.notes: Grant then turn inside the blank sentence (3.17 shape: Of course ... but), with a closing sentence that backs the resumed claim. K1 has no band-7 official items, so band_target 6. Key Of course (b1 keyed Admittedly with a Still sentence). No contrast decoy beside the concession key (excluded pair) and no In fact or Indeed. Maltese descends from Siculo-Arabic; about half its lexicon is Italian or Sicilian and a smaller share English, while grammar, numerals and kinship terms are Semitic. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

band7.why: K1 has no band-7 official items (band7 report table), so it stays a strong band 6: the grant and its "but" sit inside one sentence as in 974b5a8c, with restatement, cause and additive decoys and no contrast decoy.

items.passage: Since biologist Paul Hebert proposed it in 2003, DNA barcoding, which identifies a species by reading one short, standardized stretch of a single gene, has been widely praised as a rapid, inexpensive method for cataloging biodiversity. ______ this stretch changes so slowly in most flowering plants that closely related species often share an identical sequence. Botanists must therefore turn to other genes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence presents a widely praised claim: reading one short stretch of a gene is a fast, cheap way to identify species. The blank sentence gives a fact that limits that claim without overturning it: in most flowering plants the stretch cannot tell close relatives apart. “That said” introduces a qualification of the point just made.

A.why_wrong: The praise for barcoding does not cause the gene stretch to change slowly in plants; the slow rate of change is a limit on the method, not a result of its reputation.

B.why_wrong: The blank sentence is not a closer look at why barcoding is rapid and inexpensive; it describes a large group of organisms for which the method does not work well.

C.why_wrong: “In addition” would add another point in favor of barcoding, but the inability to separate closely related plants counts against it.

band7_moves: widely praised claim followed by a limiting fact, as in ecb31049
key outside the core 13 and no phantom-sequence or summary decoy
same-referent wrong-grain decoy (In particular) because B goes on talking about the same gene stretch
items.notes: Qualification of a praised method (ecb31049 shape: long-held view, then a fact that cuts against it); a closing sentence states the practical cost. A is a general claim, not an animals-only claim, so B reads as a limit rather than a second subject. No contrast decoy (excluded beside a concession key) and no In fact. Hebert's 2003 proposal of COI barcoding and the slow mitochondrial rate in plants (hence rbcL and matK) are textbook molecular-ecology facts. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

band7.why: Matches ecb31049: a widely praised method, then a limiting fact that is not labeled as one (identical sequences), with cause, specification and additive decoys; In particular pulls because B keeps talking about the same gene stretch. Register 5.49 chars per word. The report itself calls K2 close to band 6.

items.passage: For years after World War II, Japanese composer Tōru Takemitsu kept traditional Japanese instruments out of his music, linking their sounds to the militarism of the war years. He looked instead to French composers such as Claude Debussy. ______ in November Steps (1967), Takemitsu brought the two musical worlds together, setting the Japanese biwa and shakuhachi against a full Western orchestra.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe a long period in which Takemitsu kept Japanese instruments out of his music and modeled his work on French composers. The blank sentence gives where that path finally led: a 1967 work that brings the two musical worlds together, setting two Japanese instruments against a Western orchestra. “Ultimately” signals the eventual outcome of a long development.

B.why_wrong: Writing for the biwa and shakuhachi is not like looking to French composers or keeping Japanese instruments out of his music; it is a change in direction.

C.why_wrong: Keeping Japanese instruments out of his music did not cause Takemitsu to bring them into November Steps; the 1967 work reverses that long avoidance. It is where his development finally led, not a result that follows from the earlier sentences.

D.why_wrong: “Moreover” would add a further point of the same kind about his avoidance of Japanese music, but writing for Japanese instruments is the opposite of keeping them out of his work.

band7_moves: long development in A, its resolution in B (332e75bf)
B brings together the two musical worlds A names, so on a quick read it looks like a conclusion drawn from A (pull toward Thus)
no adversative option on offer, so the turn has to be read as an outcome
key outside the core 13; no phantom-sequence or summary decoy
items.notes: Culmination keyed Ultimately. B reverses A's habit, so a contrast word would also fit; none is offered (band-7 recipe: no plain contrast word; decoys cause, additive and a false parallel, as in 332e75bf and e225cf02). Takemitsu's postwar avoidance of Japanese music, early debt to Debussy, and November Steps for biwa, shakuhachi and orchestra (New York Philharmonic, 1967) are well documented; earlier film scores and Eclipse (1966) also used these instruments, so the passage claims only that the 1967 work came after years of avoidance. Key is the longest option (planned, batch key-longest rate). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation. Review: B rewritten as a resolution (brought the two musical worlds together) instead of a plain reversal.

fixes: blank sentence rewritten from a plain reversal ("wrote for the biwa and the shakuhachi, setting these two traditional instruments against...") to a resolution ("brought the two musical worlds together, setting the Japanese biwa and shakuhachi against..."), so Ultimately marks a culmination as in 332e75bf and Thus gets a surface pull; explanation, C why_wrong and band7_moves updated

band7.why: As drafted, B flatly reversed A, so every decoy died on that one fact and Ultimately read as a time word (6e0c60da, band 6). Now B resolves the long development by joining the two traditions A names, which reads like a conclusion and pulls Thus; no adversative is on offer. Borderline: if the gate disagrees it sits with 6e0c60da.

items.passage: Turkish novelist Orhan Pamuk’s The Museum of Innocence (2008) follows a wealthy Istanbul man who spends decades collecting objects linked to the woman he loves, including thousands of cigarette stubs she smoked, and finally exhibits them in a museum of his own. ______ in 2012 Pamuk opened a real Museum of Innocence in a nineteenth-century Istanbul house, displaying objects the novel describes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The novel is about a man who builds a museum of objects connected to the woman he loves. The blank sentence reports that the author himself later opened a real museum of those objects. “Fittingly” signals that the real museum is an apt echo of the novel it comes from.

A.why_wrong: Nothing about the novel makes a real museum surprising or unlikely; the real museum mirrors the novel instead of going against it.

B.why_wrong: The blank sentence is not a rewording of the novel’s plot; it reports a new, real-world event, Pamuk opening a museum in 2012.

D.why_wrong: “Moreover” would add another detail of the same kind to the account of the novel, but the blank sentence leaves the novel for a real museum whose point is that it matches the story.

items.notes: Aptness (3.13 shape) keyed Fittingly; P1 has no band-7 official items, so band_target 6. No cause decoy (excluded beside purpose or aptness) and no similarity decoy, since a parallel reading of novel and museum would be arguable. Novel 2008, Kemal's collection including 4,213 cigarette stubs, museum opened April 2012 in Cukurcuma, Istanbul. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

band7.why: P1 has no band-7 official items (band7 report table); a strong band-6 aptness item like 1e31470f, with Moreover as the additive decoy as there.

items.passage: Peruvian writer José María Arguedas composed every one of his novels in Spanish, the language of most of his readers, even when his characters were speaking Quechua among themselves. ______ for a 1962 hymn honoring the eighteenth-century rebel Túpac Amaru II, he wrote in Quechua, the language of his Andean childhood. Arguedas published his own Spanish translation alongside the original.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes Arguedas’s habit: he wrote his novels in Spanish. The blank sentence describes an exception to that habit: a 1962 hymn written in Quechua. “Nevertheless” signals that what follows departs from the pattern just described.

B.why_wrong: The Quechua hymn is not an example of Arguedas writing in Spanish; it is a case in which he did the opposite.

C.why_wrong: Writing his novels in Spanish, the language of most of his readers, is not a reason to write the hymn in Quechua; it points the other way.

D.why_wrong: Both sentences mention Quechua, but the hymn is not similar to the novels: the novels render Quechua conversations in Spanish, while the hymn is written in Quechua itself.

band7_moves: habit, then a one-off exception keyed Nevertheless with no other adversative option (fc95a352)
the exception is motivated (the language of his childhood) and its consequence follows (his own translation), as the spacesuits are in fc95a352
single named work in B invites the instance decoy (For example)
Quechua named in both sentences invites the false parallel (Similarly)
items.notes: Exception to a habit keyed Nevertheless (fc95a352 recipe). Only one adversative option. Arguedas wrote his novels in Spanish, rendering Quechua speech in a Quechua-shaped Spanish; his Tupac Amaru Kamaq Taytanchisman (1962) was written in Quechua and published with his own Spanish version. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

band7.why: Built on fc95a352: a habit, then a motivated one-off exception keyed Nevertheless with no other adversative option, so the hardness is the key in its exception role; Quechua in both sentences pulls Similarly and the single named work pulls For example.

items.passage: Chinese calligraphers traditionally work with a soft, tapering brush, modulating each stroke’s thickness through subtle changes in pressure. Arabic calligraphers, ______ write with a qalam, a rigid reed pen with an obliquely cut tip, so the thickness of a stroke depends primarily on the direction of the pen’s movement.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes Chinese calligraphers, who use a soft brush and vary a stroke’s thickness by pressure. The second describes Arabic calligraphers, who use a rigid pen whose stroke thickness depends on direction instead. “By contrast” marks the second group as differing from the first.

A.why_wrong: The sentence about Arabic calligraphers does not give details of the Chinese brush technique; it describes a different tool that works a different way.

B.why_wrong: “Likewise” would say Arabic calligraphers work the way Chinese calligraphers do, but a rigid reed pen controlled by direction is the opposite of a soft brush controlled by pressure.

C.why_wrong: How Chinese calligraphers use their brushes does not cause Arabic calligraphers to write with a reed pen; the two traditions are simply being compared.

items.notes: Two subjects, one attribute (what controls a stroke's thickness), opposite values; interrupter after the second subject, as in 2.6. Qalam cut with an oblique nib, stroke width set by direction; Chinese brush width set by pressure. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Fishing nets that have been lost or abandoned at sea are known as ghost nets. Drifting for years, they continue to entangle fish, sea turtles, and seabirds. ______ because most modern nets are manufactured from nylon and other synthetic plastics, they gradually shed tiny fragments as they deteriorate, contributing to the microplastics that marine animals ingest.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The passage first gives one harm of ghost nets: they keep trapping animals. The blank sentence gives a second, separate harm: as they break down, they add microplastics that animals swallow. “Moreover” adds a further point of the same kind.

A.why_wrong: Shedding plastic fragments is not a rewording of entangling animals; it is a different harm.

C.why_wrong: The second harm does not hold in spite of the first; both point the same way, showing that ghost nets damage marine life.

D.why_wrong: Breaking into microplastics is not an instance of nets entangling fish, turtles, and seabirds; it is a second, separate problem.

items.notes: Two separate harms of one thing, keyed Moreover (2.10 template), with the definition in its own sentence rather than an em dash gloss. Ghost nets keep fishing; nylon and other plastic nets fragment into microplastics. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: In his Dream Pool Essays (1088), Chinese scholar Shen Kuo provided the earliest surviving description of a magnetized needle compass, noting that the needle pointed slightly east of due south. ______ having discovered fossilized seashells in cliffs far inland, he proposed that the surrounding land had been built up over ages from silt deposited by rivers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence names one contribution in Shen Kuo’s book: a description of the magnetic compass. The blank sentence names a second, unrelated contribution: a theory of how land is formed from river silt. “Additionally” adds another item to the list of his achievements.

A.why_wrong: Describing the compass needle did not lead Shen Kuo to his theory about land built from silt; the fossil seashells did.

B.why_wrong: Nothing about the compass description makes the land theory surprising; the two sentences simply list two of his contributions.

D.why_wrong: The theory about silt and fossil seashells is not a rewording of the compass description; it is a separate idea about geology.

items.notes: Two separate contributions by one person (2.11 and 1.7 pattern), keyed Additionally. Dream Pool Essays (1088): magnetized needle pointing south with a slight eastward deviation; marine shells in the Taihang cliffs and land built from river silt. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Among the Mosuo, a small ethnic group living near Lugu Lake in southwestern China, households are traditionally matrilineal—______ family membership is traced through mothers rather than fathers, so that children belong to their mother’s household. Each household is headed by a senior woman, who manages its land and finances.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first part of the sentence uses the technical term “matrilineal.” The part after the blank says the same thing in plainer words: family membership passes through mothers, so children belong to the mother’s household. “That is” introduces a rewording of what came just before.

B.why_wrong: Tracing family through mothers does not go against the claim that Mosuo households are matrilineal; it is what that word means.

C.why_wrong: “Similarly” would introduce a second, comparable case, but the clause after the blank describes the same Mosuo households again in other words.

D.why_wrong: The clause after the blank is not one instance of matrilineal practice; it states the general rule that the term names.

items.notes: Technical term, then a plain rewording after an em dash (2.15 shape), with a following sentence that adds a new fact so the rewording stands apart. No specification decoy beside the restatement key (it would be arguable here). Mosuo households are matrilineal, children belong to the mother's household, and a senior woman (dabu) heads it. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: In parts of Alaska and Siberia, black spruce forests grow on permafrost, ground that has remained frozen for thousands of years. As rising temperatures thaw this ice-rich soil, it collapses unevenly beneath the trees’ shallow roots. ______ the spruces lean at odd angles in every direction, forming what scientists call “drunken forests.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence says that thawing permafrost collapses unevenly under the spruces’ shallow roots. The blank sentence gives the result: the trees tilt at odd angles. “Hence” introduces a consequence of what was just described.

A.why_wrong: The trees do not lean in spite of the ground collapsing beneath them; they lean because of it.

B.why_wrong: Leaning trees are not an instance of soil collapsing; they are what the collapsing soil causes.

D.why_wrong: The leaning trees are not a second case like the collapsing ground; the passage links the two as cause and effect.

items.notes: Condition, mechanism, consequence over three sentences (2.14 pattern), keyed Hence. Drunken forests: thawing ice-rich permafrost (thermokarst) tilts shallow-rooted black spruce in Alaska, Canada and Siberia. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: In 1934, the Turkish parliament passed the Surname Law, requiring every citizen to adopt a hereditary family name and register it officially. ______ most people in Turkey had been identified by a given name alone, frequently supplemented by a nickname, a patronymic, or an honorific title such as “Bey” or “Pasha.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes a 1934 law requiring family names. The blank sentence, in the past perfect, describes how people were identified before that law. “Previously” signals that the second sentence refers to an earlier time.

A.why_wrong: The 1934 law could not have caused people to be known by given names alone; that practice came before the law.

C.why_wrong: Being known by a given name and a title is not an instance of adopting a family name; it describes the practice the law replaced.

D.why_wrong: Using given names and titles is not similar to adopting family names; the second sentence describes the earlier, different system.

items.notes: Dated change, then the earlier state described in the past perfect (2.2 shape), keyed Previously. No adversative decoy: with no earlier practice stated in the first sentence, however would read as acceptable. Turkey's Surname Law of 21 June 1934; before it, given names with titles such as Bey, Pasha, Efendi, nicknames or a father's name. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: With their dense, brightly colored hair and their tendency to scurry across exposed ground, velvet ants closely resemble oversized, fuzzy ants. Entomologists, ______ classify them as wasps: the wingless females are the individuals typically observed running about, whereas the males of most species possess wings and fly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says velvet ants look like large, fuzzy ants. The second gives the experts’ view that goes against this appearance: they are actually wasps. “Though” signals that the second sentence contrasts with the first.

A.why_wrong: Looking like ants is not the reason entomologists classify velvet ants as wasps; the classification goes against their appearance.

B.why_wrong: Classifying velvet ants as wasps is not an instance of their resembling ants; it is a different, opposing point.

C.why_wrong: “Similarly” would mean entomologists also treat velvet ants as ants, but they classify them as wasps.

items.notes: Appearance, then specialists' view, with the contrast word as an interrupter after the subject (2.16 shape). Option set varied from 2.16's. Velvet ants (Mutillidae) are wasps; females wingless, males of most species winged. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Dutch engineers sought to protect Rotterdam from North Sea storm surges without obstructing the heavily trafficked shipping channel connecting the city’s port to the sea. ______ they constructed the Maeslantkering, a barrier whose two enormous hinged arms rest in dry docks along the riverbanks and swing shut across the channel only when a dangerous surge is forecast.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence states the engineers’ goal: protect Rotterdam from storm surges while keeping the shipping channel open. The blank sentence describes what they built to meet that goal: a barrier that closes only when a surge is coming. “To that end” introduces an action taken to achieve a stated goal.

B.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not sum up what came before; it introduces new information, the barrier the engineers built.

C.why_wrong: Building the barrier does not go against the engineers’ aim; it carries that aim out.

D.why_wrong: Building the barrier is not a second, comparable case alongside the engineers’ goal; it is the means of reaching that goal.

items.notes: Goal, then the deliberate act that serves it, keyed To that end (3.15 relation at medium; the only medium P1 official, 2.5, keys Fittingly). No cause decoy (excluded beside purpose); In sum as in 3.15, with contrast and false-parallel decoys. Key is the longest option (planned, batch key-longest rate). Maeslantkering on the Nieuwe Waterweg, completed 1997, two floating sector-gate arms stored in dry docks on the banks, closed only for forecast high surges. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Polish paper cutouts, known as wycinanki, have traditionally decorated rural homes, especially around Easter. Their designs vary considerably from region to region. ______ cutouts from the area surrounding Łowicz, in central Poland, are built up from many layers of brightly colored paper and often depict roosters, flowers, or village celebrations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence makes a general claim: wycinanki designs differ from region to region. The blank sentence describes the style of one region, Łowicz. “For example” introduces a specific case of the general claim.

A.why_wrong: The Łowicz style does not go against the claim that designs vary by region; it is one of the regional styles.

B.why_wrong: Regional variety does not cause Łowicz cutouts to be layered and brightly colored; the Łowicz style illustrates the variety rather than resulting from it.

D.why_wrong: “Regardless” would mean the Łowicz style has nothing to do with regional variety, but it is one of the regional styles the passage describes.

items.notes: General claim with a regional quantifier, then one named instance (1.25 pattern, three sentences). Lowicz wycinanki are multicolored and layered, with roosters, flowers and folk scenes; Kurpie cutouts are single-color. Key is the longest option (planned, batch key-longest rate). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Several fish species migrate upstream by climbing waterfalls, clinging to slippery rock while water pours over them. ______ the ʻoʻopu nōpili, a small goby found only in Hawaiian streams, ascends waterfalls by alternately gripping the rock with its mouth and with a suction disk formed by its fused pelvic fins.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says that several kinds of fish climb waterfalls. The blank sentence names one such fish, the ʻoʻopu nōpili, and explains how it climbs. “For instance” introduces a specific example of the general statement.

A.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not reword the first sentence; it adds a particular fish and new details about how it climbs.

C.why_wrong: The goby’s climbing does not contrast with the claim that some fish climb waterfalls; it is a case of that claim.

D.why_wrong: The passage describes what these fish do, not events in time, so nothing in the blank sentence happened before the first sentence.

items.notes: General claim with a quantifier (several fish species), then one named instance. Sicyopterus stimpsoni (o'opu nopili), endemic Hawaiian goby, climbs waterfalls by inching with its oral sucker and pelvic disk. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: In 1995, Swiss astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced the discovery of 51 Pegasi b. It was the first planet ever detected orbiting a Sun-like star beyond our solar system. ______ in 2019, the two astronomers were awarded a share of the Nobel Prize in Physics for this discovery.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The passage moves from the 1995 discovery to the 2019 Nobel Prize awarded for it. “Later” signals that the event in the blank sentence happened after the one described before it.

A.why_wrong: The Nobel Prize is not an example of the discovery of 51 Pegasi b; it is an event that came years after it.

B.why_wrong: Receiving a prize for the discovery is not a second event like the discovery itself; it is a later event that honors it.

C.why_wrong: Winning a Nobel Prize for the discovery does not contrast with making it; it follows from it.

items.notes: Dated events in order, keyed Later (1.18 shape). No cause decoy: as a result would be defensible, since the prize was awarded for the discovery. 51 Pegasi b announced 1995; Mayor and Queloz shared half of the 2019 physics prize (with James Peebles), hence a share. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Bògòlanfini, or mud cloth, is a traditional textile from Mali. To make it, artisans first soak handwoven cotton in a solution of crushed n’gallama leaves, which dyes the fabric yellow. ______ they paint designs onto the cloth using mud fermented for months; iron in the mud reacts chemically with the leaf dye, producing dark brown or black patterns.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence gives the first step in making mud cloth, marked by “first”: soaking the cotton in a leaf dye. The blank sentence gives the step after that: painting designs with fermented mud. “Then” introduces the next step in a process.

B.why_wrong: Painting with mud is not an example of soaking cloth in leaf dye; it is the next step.

C.why_wrong: Painting designs does not contradict the soaking step; it builds on it, since the mud reacts with the leaf dye.

D.why_wrong: Painting with mud is not done in the same way as soaking in a leaf bath; it is a different step that follows it.

items.notes: Process with a first-step cue, keyed Then (1.11 shape). Bogolanfini: cotton soaked in a decoction of n'gallama (Anogeissus) leaves, painted with iron-rich fermented mud that darkens where it reacts with the tannins. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Tristan da Cunha, a volcanic island in the South Atlantic Ocean, lies more than 2,400 kilometers from Cape Town, South Africa. Its mountainous terrain provides no suitable location for an airstrip. ______ the island’s approximately 250 residents can travel to the mainland only by ship, a voyage lasting roughly six days.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences say the island is very remote and has no place for an airstrip. The blank sentence gives the consequence: residents can reach the mainland only by ship. “As a result” introduces an effect of what came before.

A.why_wrong: “Regardless” would mean the lack of an airstrip has nothing to do with travel by ship, but it is the reason ships are the only option.

B.why_wrong: Traveling only by ship is not similar to the island lacking an airstrip; it follows from it.

D.why_wrong: The passage is not listing steps or points in order; the blank sentence gives a consequence of the island’s isolation.

items.notes: Condition, then its consequence for the people involved, keyed As a result. Tristan da Cunha: about 2,400 km from Cape Town, no airstrip, about 250 residents, roughly six days by ship. Key is the longest option (planned, batch key-longest rate). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Many Mongolian herders relocate their camps several times annually, following fresh pasture for their sheep, goats, horses, and cattle. ______ the traditional Mongolian dwelling, the ger, is designed for easy dismantling: its felt coverings and collapsible wooden frame can be taken down in an hour or two and carried by a few camels or a truck.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says that many Mongolian herders move their camps several times a year. The blank sentence gives a consequence of that way of life: their traditional home is built to be taken apart and moved quickly. “Consequently” introduces a result of what was just described.

A.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not reword the first sentence; it gives new information about the design of the ger.

C.why_wrong: A home that is easy to move does not contrast with frequent moves; it suits them.

D.why_wrong: The blank sentence is not a summary of the passage; it introduces new details about how the ger is built.

items.notes: Way of life, then the design it leads to, keyed Consequently. Ger: felt over a collapsible lattice frame, taken down in about an hour or two and moved by camels, yaks or truck. items.passage: Completed in 1965, the Akosombo Dam on Ghana’s Volta River still generates a substantial share of the country’s electricity. ______ when the dam’s reservoir, Lake Volta, filled, it flooded hundreds of villages and forced about 80,000 people to leave their homes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives a benefit of the Akosombo Dam: it supplies much of Ghana’s electricity. The blank sentence gives a serious cost of the same dam: its reservoir displaced about 80,000 people. “However” signals a contrast between the benefit and the cost.

A.why_wrong: Generating electricity is not the reason the reservoir flooded villages; the flooding happened when the lake formed behind the dam.

B.why_wrong: Displacing thousands of people is not similar to supplying electricity; it is a harm set against that benefit.

C.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not sum up the passage; it adds a new fact about the dam, the flooding of villages.

items.notes: Positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject (1.33 shape), keyed However. Akosombo completed 1965; Lake Volta flooded about 740 villages and displaced about 78,000 people; the dam remains a major share of Ghana's generation. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: In many Western homes, framed paintings remain in the same position on a wall for years. ______ a Japanese hanging scroll, or kakemono, is typically displayed for only a few weeks. It is then rolled up and replaced with another scroll appropriate to the upcoming season.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says framed paintings in Western homes stay in one place for years. The blank sentence says a Japanese hanging scroll is shown for only a few weeks. “By contrast” signals that the two kinds of artwork are treated in opposite ways.

A.why_wrong: A Japanese scroll shown for a few weeks is not an instance of a painting left in place for years; it is the opposite custom.

B.why_wrong: How Western homes display paintings does not cause Japanese scrolls to be changed every few weeks.

D.why_wrong: A scroll shown for a few weeks is the opposite of a painting left in place for years, not something similar.

items.notes: Two subjects, one attribute (how long an artwork stays on display), opposite values, keyed By contrast, with a follow-up sentence after the blank. Kakemono are rotated in the tokonoma by season or occasion. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Kenyan author Grace Ogot published her first novel, The Promised Land, in 1966; like many of her short stories, it draws on the folktales, history, and customs of her Luo community in western Kenya. ______ she served in Kenya’s national parliament during the 1980s, representing the Gem constituency in Siaya District.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes Ogot’s work as a writer. The blank sentence adds a second, separate achievement: her service in Kenya’s parliament. “In addition” introduces another item of the same kind, here another part of her career.

B.why_wrong: Serving in parliament did not replace her writing; the passage presents it as a further achievement.

C.why_wrong: Writing novels and stories drawn on Luo folktales did not cause Ogot to serve in parliament; the two are separate parts of her career.

D.why_wrong: The blank sentence describes service during the 1980s, so “Today” does not fit the time it refers to.

items.notes: Two acts by one person (1.7 pattern), keyed In addition. Grace Ogot (1930-2015): The Promised Land (1966), Luo-based stories; member of parliament for Gem in the 1980s and assistant minister. Key is the longest option (planned, batch key-longest rate). items.passage: Brazilian painter Beatriz Milhazes creates vibrant, densely layered canvases. She relies on a transfer technique she developed in the late 1980s. ______ she paints each motif, such as a flower or a circle, onto a transparent plastic sheet, presses the wet paint against the canvas, and then peels the plastic away, leaving the image behind.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence mentions a transfer technique without saying what it involves. The blank sentence spells out exactly what Milhazes does: paints on plastic, presses it to the canvas, and peels it away. “Specifically” introduces the precise details of something just mentioned.

A.why_wrong: The steps in the blank sentence do not go against the transfer technique; they describe it.

C.why_wrong: The blank sentence is not a second, similar technique; it is the same technique explained in detail.

D.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not sum up the passage; it adds new details about the technique.

items.notes: General mention, then its exact content (1.19 shape), keyed Specifically; no example decoy beside a specification key. Milhazes's monotransfer method, developed around 1989: motifs painted on plastic sheets and transferred to canvas. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.
